h1: Industrial Axial Exhaust Fan for Kitchens and Ducts
short_description: A smoky, hot kitchen slows your staff and stains your walls. It is built for long daily running in commercial kitchens, workshops and stores across Kenya. It is the extractor fan we fit to most of our kitchen hoods.

sections.heading: Key Features and Benefits
sections.body:
Six-blade axial design. Moves a lot of air efficiently along short and medium ducts, so smoke clears quickly and the kitchen stays cooler.

Motor inside a compact cylindrical casing. Fits in line with round ductwork, saving space.

Base feet and airflow arrow. Bolt it securely to a platform or bracket, and install it the right way first time.

sections.heading: Who It Suits and Where It Is Used
sections.body: It suits restaurant and hotel kitchens with a canopy hood, school and hospital kitchens, bakeries, laundries and workshops that need to remove heat, steam or fumes, and warehouses and stores that need better airflow.

sections.heading: How It Works with a Kitchen Hood
sections.body: A hood on its own only collects smoke and grease. The exhaust fan is what pulls that air through the grease filters, along the duct and out of the building. Without a fan of the right size, smoke spills out of the hood and fills the kitchen. When we supply a hood, we can advise on the fan and duct to match it.

sections.heading: Axial vs Centrifugal Fans
sections.body: Axial fans move a large volume of air and are simple and affordable, which makes them a good choice for straight, short duct runs. Centrifugal fans build more pressure and suit long duct runs with many bends. If your duct is long or complex, talk to us before choosing.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
sections.body: Measure the duct diameter and the length of the run to the outside. Check the size of the hood or room you want to ventilate. Plan the power supply with an electrician, and decide where the air will discharge so it does not blow into a neighbour's window.

sections.heading: Installation Tips
sections.body: Fit the fan with the airflow arrow pointing towards the outlet. Use flexible connectors to reduce vibration and noise. Make sure there is an access point for cleaning, because kitchen exhaust carries grease that builds up on the blades.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body: Switch off and isolate the power before any work. Clean grease from the blades and casing regularly; a greasy fan is less efficient and a fire risk. Check the mounting bolts and listen for unusual noise, which can mean a worn bearing.

sections.heading: Who It Suits and Where It Is Used
sections.body: It suits restaurants and hotels, school, college and hospital kitchens, fast food outlets with fryers and grills, and bakeries and catering kitchens.

sections.heading: Baffle Filters vs Mesh Filters
sections.body: Mesh filters trap grease in fine layers of wire and clog quickly, which reduces airflow. Baffle filters use overlapping steel channels that make the air turn sharply, so grease drops out and drains away. They clog less, are easier to clean and resist flames better, which is why they are the standard choice for commercial kitchens with fryers and grills.

sections.heading: Why Every Commercial Kitchen Needs a Hood
sections.body: Cooking on a commercial scale produces heat, smoke and airborne grease. Without a hood, grease settles on walls, ceilings and lights, smoke irritates staff and the kitchen becomes uncomfortably hot. A properly sized hood keeps the air clearer, protects the building and reduces the fire risk from grease build-up. Health inspectors also look for good ventilation.

sections.heading: Sizing Your Hood
sections.body: The hood should be longer than the cooking line it covers, with some overhang at each end and at the front, so smoke does not escape. Measure the full length of your cookers, fryers and grills, and the height from the floor to the ceiling. We make hoods to suit your kitchen.

sections.heading: Complete Ventilation System
sections.body: A hood works with ductwork and an exhaust fan. We can supply the fan and duct together with the hood, so all the parts are matched and the system pulls enough air.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body: Remove the baffle filters and wash them in hot soapy water or a dishwasher regularly; in busy kitchens, weekly or more often. Wipe the canopy inside and out. Have the duct cleaned by a professional from time to time, because grease in ducts is a fire hazard.

faqs.q: Where can I buy a wall mounted hand wash trough in Kenya?
faqs.a: Kitchen And All sells it online at kitchenandall.co.ke, and our team is ready to advise you on the right option. We deliver free within Nairobi and quickly countrywide with shipping charges.

faqs.q: Can I get a pedal operated hand wash sink?
faqs.a: Yes. We make hand wash sinks with foot pedal or knee operated taps on request. Ask us for the option that suits your facility.

faqs.q: Are the taps hands-free?
faqs.a: Yes. Elbow-lever taps are operated with the elbow or forearm.

faqs.q: Does it need a strong wall?
faqs.a: Yes. It hangs on brackets, so the wall must carry its weight.

faqs.q: Can I get more stations?
faqs.a: Ask us about longer troughs with more taps.
